articles.surfaceLabel: Does Switzerland's Privacy Law Apply to Your Organization?
articles.plainSummary: Switzerland's revised privacy law took effect in September 2023. It applies to processing that has an effect in Switzerland, even when the organization is based abroad, and it covers private companies and federal bodies.
articles.personalImpact: Switzerland has long treated privacy as part of personal dignity, not just paperwork. Yet your data still flows to banks, insurers, and online services daily. The revised FADP covers private organizations and federal bodies whose handling of data affects people in Switzerland. Cantonal and communal bodies follow cantonal law instead.
articles.professionalLayer: The revised FADP modernized Swiss data protection to maintain alignment with European standards while keeping a distinctly Swiss structure. It applies to circumstances that have an effect in Switzerland, even if initiated abroad, giving it extraterritorial reach. Foreign controllers meeting certain thresholds must designate a Swiss representative. Like the GDPR, and unlike the old Swiss law, it protects only natural persons. Unlike the GDPR, it has no general prohibition model. It enforces mainly through criminal fines of up to CHF 250,000 on responsible individuals, and only for intentional breaches. Most offenses are prosecuted only if someone files a complaint. A business itself can be fined up to CHF 50,000 when finding the responsible person would take disproportionate effort. Cantonal authorities prosecute and impose these fines. The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner supervises compliance and can investigate and issue binding orders.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your processing have effects in Switzerland, and if so, have you assessed FADP obligations separately from the GDPR rather than assuming equivalence?

gapRemediation.smb: GDPR compliance covers much of the FADP, but confirm Swiss specifics: the representative requirement, Swiss breach duties, and criminal liability of individuals.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Assign ownership for Swiss requirements. The personal criminal liability model changes who inside the organization carries risk.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Treat Switzerland as its own compliance track with counsel familiar with FADP criminal provisions, not a GDPR footnote.

comparisonFlags.note: FADP fines are criminal penalties on responsible individuals, up to CHF 250,000, and require intent. A business can be fined up to CHF 50,000 where identifying the responsible person would take disproportionate effort.

articles.surfaceLabel: When Swiss Law Allows Your Data to Be Used
articles.plainSummary: Swiss law works differently from the GDPR. Private organizations may generally process personal data without a specific legal basis, as long as they follow the processing principles and do not unlawfully harm the person's privacy.
articles.personalImpact: A company cannot treat your data as freely usable simply because it holds it. Under Swiss law, processing must respect your personality and stay within a justifiable purpose. Consent, a contract, or an overriding interest can justify it.
articles.professionalLayer: The FADP does not adopt the GDPR's prohibition-with-legal-bases model. Private-sector processing is permitted by default if it complies with the processing principles: lawfulness, good faith, proportionality, purpose limitation and recognizability, storage limitation, accuracy, and security. Processing that breaches the principles, goes against the data subject's express wish, or discloses sensitive data to third parties is a personality violation. It then needs justification by consent, an overriding private or public interest, or law. Where consent is relied on, it must be informed and voluntary. It must be explicit for sensitive data or high-risk profiling. Federal bodies, by contrast, need a statutory basis. This inverts the GDPR model.
articles.assessTrigger: Do you know which of your Swiss processing activities breach a principle, go against someone's express wish, or disclose sensitive data to third parties, and so need justification?

gapRemediation.smb: Follow the processing principles. Where you rely on consent for sensitive data, make it explicit. You do not need to map every activity to a legal basis as under the GDPR.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Document where you rely on justification grounds, especially overriding interest, since those calls carry the legal weight the GDPR puts on legal bases.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Keep Swiss records distinguishing principle-based processing from justified processing, and review high-risk profiling consents explicitly.

comparisonFlags.note: The FADP permits private processing by default under principles. The GDPR prohibits processing unless a legal basis applies.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to See Your Data in Switzerland
articles.plainSummary: You can ask any organization whether it processes personal data about you and receive a copy, generally free of charge. The organization normally has 30 days to respond.
articles.personalImpact: Insurers and creditworthiness agencies quietly build a picture that shapes your rates and approvals. Much of it stays out of your sight. This right lets you request everything an organization holds about you.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 25 grants data subjects the right to obtain the information needed to assert their rights and to confirm transparent processing. The mandatory minimum includes the controller's identity, the data processed, purposes, retention, origin, recipients, and, where applicable, the existence of automated individual decisions and their logic. Information must generally be provided within 30 days, free of charge, subject to narrow exceptions. Refusal, restriction, or delay is permitted only on legal grounds such as overriding third-party interests. The law also lets controllers refuse requests that are obviously unjustified, such as those that do not serve data protection or are clearly frivolous. Reasons must be given.
articles.responseTimeline: 30 days from receipt as the standard deadline.
articles.assessTrigger: Can you fulfill Swiss access requests within 30 days, including the FADP's mandatory minimum information set?

gapRemediation.smb: A response template covering the Article 25 minimum items is a reasonable starting point. Track the 30-day deadline.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Align your GDPR DSR workflow to also emit the FADP minimum set, which differs slightly from Article 15 content.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Route Swiss requests through your DSR platform with an FADP-specific template and refusal-grounds logging.

articles.surfaceLabel: What Happens When Your Data Is Compromised in Switzerland
articles.plainSummary: Organizations must report data breaches that are likely to create high risk for affected people to the Swiss regulator as quickly as possible. There is no fixed 72-hour deadline like in the EU.
articles.personalImpact: A breach can expose your financial and health details, areas Switzerland guards closely. Silence from a company only deepens the harm. Swiss law requires prompt notice to the FDPIC when the risk to you is high. You are told where that is needed to protect you, or where the regulator asks.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 24 requires controllers to notify the FDPIC as soon as possible of breaches likely to lead to a high risk to the data subject's personality or fundamental rights. This is a higher threshold and a softer deadline than the GDPR, which requires notice within 72 hours where feasible unless a breach is unlikely to pose a risk. Data subjects must be informed where necessary for their protection or where the FDPIC requests it. The controller may limit, delay, or skip that notice in some cases, such as when a public announcement does the same job. Processors must report breaches to controllers as soon as possible. Notifications to the FDPIC are made through its online portal, and the notification itself cannot be used against the notifier in criminal proceedings without consent. Since April 2025, the FDPIC may forward a report to the Federal Office for Cybersecurity, with the controller's consent.
articles.responseTimeline: FDPIC: as soon as possible where high risk exists. Individuals: where necessary for their protection, or if the FDPIC requests it.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your breach process apply the Swiss high-risk threshold and FDPIC portal route, distinct from your EU 72-hour workflow?

gapRemediation.smb: Add the FDPIC portal to your breach checklist and note the high-risk threshold.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Define who assesses the Swiss high-risk threshold, since it differs from the GDPR trigger your team may default to.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Encode jurisdiction-specific thresholds and clocks into the incident workflow so Swiss and EU notifications are decided separately.

comparisonFlags.note: The FADP requires notification as soon as possible only for high-risk breaches. The GDPR requires notice within 72 hours where feasible, unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk.

articles.surfaceLabel: Moving Personal Data Out of Switzerland
articles.plainSummary: Personal data may leave Switzerland freely only to countries the Swiss government lists as adequate. For other destinations, organizations need safeguards such as approved contract clauses.
articles.personalImpact: Your data often leaves Switzerland for servers elsewhere. Abroad, it may fall under weaker protection. Swiss law allows the transfer only where adequate safeguards remain in place.
articles.professionalLayer: Cross-border disclosure is permitted where the Federal Council has listed the destination state as providing adequate protection, a list published in an annex to the ordinance. Absent adequacy, transfers require safeguards including standard data protection clauses accepted by the FDPIC, where the EU SCCs adapted for Switzerland are common practice, binding corporate rules approved by the FDPIC, codes of conduct or certification, or specific derogations such as explicit consent or contract performance. Since September 2024, the US counts as adequate for organizations certified under the Swiss-US Data Privacy Framework.
articles.assessTrigger: Do your transfers out of Switzerland rely on the Federal Council adequacy list or Swiss-adapted clauses, rather than EU paperwork alone?

gapRemediation.smb: Where you use EU SCCs, add the Swiss adaptation language most vendors provide.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Inventory Swiss-origin flows separately and confirm each rests on the Swiss adequacy list or adapted clauses.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Maintain Swiss transfer documentation alongside EU and UK tracks, and monitor the Federal Council adequacy list for changes.
